paragraphs: Critics of the period tended to treat the landscape painter Elise Marchand's late canvases as evidence of declining powers. Their sparse compositions and muted palette were read as signs of fatigue, a reading that hardened into orthodoxy within a generation. Yet her surviving letters suggest a different explanation. Marchand wrote repeatedly of her wish to 'subtract' from each picture until only the essential remained, and she destroyed several early studies that she judged too ornate. If this reading of the letters is right, the late style was a deliberate refinement and not a retreat. I would go further and suggest, though I cannot prove it, that her pared-down manner anticipated tastes that did not become fashionable until decades after her death.
